newsitem.title: JAPAN: JGBs sharply weaker by late Tokyo trading.
newsitem.headline: JGBs sharply weaker by late Tokyo trading.

text.p: Japanese government bond (JGB) cash and futures were sharply weaker by late Tokyo trading on Wednesday due to corrective sales following recent gains and hedge-selling by dealers and investors.
The key December ended at 125.60, down sharply from Tuesday's 126.40.

In morning trade, the postal savings system, one of Japan's largest institutional investors, unloaded the 170th eight-year bonds for three-year JGBs, accentuating losses at the longer end of the market.
Other institutional investors were also detected engaging in similar activity, or shortening average maturities in portfolios to hedge against losses at the long end.
In the interest rate swap (IRS) market, a powerful long-term bank paid a one-year fixed rate, pushing up the IRS rate across the curve, traders said.
One-year IRS rate was quoted at 0.63-0.67 percent, up from 0.59/0.63 percent in late trading on Tuesday.
Meanwhile, foreign speculators appeared to have received fixed interest rates and placed hedge selling orders in the JGB futures market, deepening losses in the market, traders said.
Local life insurers were on the offer side in the cash JGB market, particularly in the longer-end, traders said.
The yield of the key 182nd 10-year JGB was at 2.505 percent, up from 2.435 percent on Tuesday and compared with the record-low 2.415 percent yield for any benchmark cash JGBs also set on Tuesday.

Bank of Japan Governor Yasuo Matsushita said in a speech on Wednesday that Japan's economy was continuing to recover gradually but factors such as competition from Asian economies and balance-sheet adjustments were hindering the pace of that recovery.
He said corporate capital investment, although recovering gradually, had not yet recovered completely due to stock adjustments and debt repayments.
Matsushita said a flow of cheap imports from Asia had contributed to an decrease in capital investment within Japan.
Matsushita's remark, although bullish for bonds in theory, was overwhelmed by Wednesday's bearish market sentiment, traders said.
